title: Al-Biruni on fairness
hookLine: he writes that he will set out the views of others as they are, without distortion (India)
tomorrow: can you fight someone's army and still call some of them friends?

lines: HALF A SENTENCE, CUT TO LOOK DUMB.
A TEACHER READS A TWISTED BOOK.
WRITE IT THE WAY THEY'D SAY IT.
cards: A clip goes around: half a sentence from someone on the other side, cut so it sounds ridiculous. The replies pile on. Nobody goes back for the whole sentence.
Al-Biruni, a Muslim scholar, opens his book on India in a scene like that.
He's with his teacher, and they're reading a writer who describes the beliefs of a Muslim school, the Mu'tazila, and twists them until they look foolish. His teacher is unhappy about it.
So he asks al-Biruni for something harder than a reply: write down what the people of India believe, the way they themselves would say it.

teach.b: So he does. His book sets out Hindu beliefs, books, sciences and customs, and in the preface he names his rule plainly: he will set out the views of others as they are, without distortion.
This book, he says, is not a polemic, not an argument against anyone. Where Hindu thinkers say something close to the Greek philosophers, he sets the two side by side so readers can see the likeness.
When a belief sounds strange to his Muslim readers, he often separates what the learned hold from what ordinary people say, a line you could draw in any people, his own included.
He doesn't hide that he's a Muslim, or that he disagrees in places. He just keeps two jobs apart: first describe, then discuss. He's honest about how hard the first job is.
In his opening chapter he names the walls between peoples: language, religion, customs, and old suspicion on both sides.
The Qur'an had already set the bar: don't let hatred of a people pull you away from justice.
Here's the thing worth telling a friend tonight: a careful account of Hindu thought, written by a Muslim who made fairness the rule.
Fair doesn't mean agreeing. It means a Hindu reader could recognize their own belief in your words. Then, and only then, you've earned the right to disagree.

how: Muslim students of other religions still read al-Biruni's book on India; teachers who follow him describe another faith from its own books and people before discussing it.

o: keeping quiet about any belief you don't share
proving another religion wrong with polite arguments
describing others' beliefs the way they'd describe them

games.q: the book and its rule — tap the pairs.
p: views set out as they are

s: al-Biruni wrote his book on India to argue Hindus out of their beliefs
he says it is not a polemic: he sets out their views as they are.
where Hindu and Greek thinkers were alike, he put them side by side
so readers could see the likeness for themselves.
being fair to a view means you secretly agree with it
fair means its holders would recognize it in your words. you can still disagree, afterward.

games.q: your aunt keeps a strict diet you think is silly. at dinner a cousin asks you why she eats that way. what does al-Biruni's rule ask of you?
o: call it a fad, but kindly, so nobody's feelings get hurt.
give her reasons the way she would, then your view if asked.
change the subject; explaining it could sound like agreeing.
games.why: first describe, then discuss. al-Biruni set out others' views as they are, and only then said where he differed.

practice: Choose one view you disagree with, a real one, from a friend, a relative, or the news. Write it down by hand in one sentence, the way its best defender would put it. Read it back slowly: would they nod?

wordCard.voice: Al-Biruni on fairness: a Muslim scholar who wrote down the beliefs of India as their own people held them, and kept his arguments for later.

orig.note: Arabic: insaf, fairness, giving each side its due.

carryVoice: To keep: as they are, a fair hearing before any answer. Seven stops on the road, one to go.

sources.ref: al-Biruni, Kitab fi Tahqiq ma li-l-Hind (India), preface: the teacher's complaint about a distorted account of the Mu'tazila; the promise to set out the Hindus' views as they are, not as a polemic, with Greek parallels
al-Biruni, India, chapter 1 (the barriers between peoples: language, religion, customs, mutual suspicion)
Qur'an 5:8 (let not hatred of a people make you deal unjustly)
